current_recheck.methodSummary: Contre-revue en lecture seule des quatre chemins actuels désignés par formation-manifest.json, du rapport initial et de p0-p2-remediation-manifest.json. Les chemins de rendu/progression LessonViewer.tsx, chapterProgress.ts, blockRegistry.ts et learningDesign.ts ont été lus. Chaque constat initial a été rapproché de la donnée courante et du chemin de rendu applicable. Une correction n’est créditée que si la donnée et le composant démontrent le résultat apprenant ; un retrait n’est crédité que s’il figure dans le manifeste de retraits. Ainsi, les trois objectifs vidéo ajoutés et effectivement transmis/affichés sont resolved_with_evidence. Les douze checkpoints disparus des cours 02–04 sont externally_unverifiable, et non « résolus » : aucune trace de retrait de cette formation ni équivalence pédagogique n’est fournie. Score : 77/100. Base = moyenne non arrondie des 96 scores de chapitres du rapport initial (71,02), arrondie à 71 ; +2 points pour chacune des trois corrections P2 prouvées (= +6), arrondi à 77. Les 13 constats still_open et les 12 constats externally_unverifiable ne reçoivent aucun crédit ; aucune absence d’écran n’augmente la note. Le score ne certifie ni le visionnage des vidéos, ni l’exactitude réglementaire, ni une exécution navigateur authentifiée de bout en bout.

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

• Define the core principles that constitute trustworthy AI and explain why they matter for organizations.
• Identify the key frameworks and guidelines published by leading bodies such as the EU, OECD, and NIST.
• Explain how principles like fairness, transparency, and accountability translate into practical AI development and deployment decisions.
• Recognize the relationship between trustworthy AI principles and regulatory compliance obligations.

Trustworthy AI refers to systems that are lawful, ethical, and technically robust throughout their entire lifecycle. Major international bodies have converged on a shared set of principles: fairness and non-discrimination ensure AI does not perpetuate or amplify bias; transparency and explainability require that decisions be understandable to affected stakeholders; privacy and data governance protect individual rights; safety and robustness demand that systems perform reliably under varied conditions; and accountability establishes clear lines of responsibility for outcomes.

The EU AI Act and OECD AI Principles operationalize these values into policy, while NIST's AI Risk Management Framework provides practical implementation guidance. Organizations that embed these principles early in design reduce regulatory exposure, build public trust, and improve long-term system performance.

Trustworthy AI is not a checklist but a continuous, organization-wide commitment.

• Fairness & Non-Discrimination: AI systems must treat individuals and groups equitably, avoiding biased outcomes based on protected characteristics such as race, gender, or age.

• Transparency & Explainability: Stakeholders must be able to understand how an AI system reaches its conclusions, enabling meaningful oversight and challenge.

• Accountability: Organizations and individuals must accept responsibility for the design, deployment, and consequences of AI systems, supported by auditable documentation.

• Human Oversight: Trustworthy AI preserves meaningful human control, ensuring that automated decisions can be reviewed, corrected, or overridden when necessary.

question.en: Which of the following best describes the principle of 'explainability' in trustworthy AI?

text.en: Ensuring that AI systems are only used by qualified engineers
Making AI decision-making processes understandable to affected stakeholders
Encrypting AI model weights to protect intellectual property

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) The purpose and structure of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) core and crosscutting functions—Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.
- 2) How trustworthiness characteristics (valid/reliable, safe, secure/resilient, accountable/transparent, explainable/interpretable, privacy-enhanced, and fair with harmful bias managed) translate into requirements and controls.
- 3) Practical artifacts, roles, and processes to operationalize the framework across the AI lifecycle.

body.en:
The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary, risk-based, socio-technical framework to help organizations design, develop, deploy, and use trustworthy AI. It defines a crosscutting Govern function and three lifecycle functions—Map, Measure, and Manage—that work together to identify, assess, and treat AI risk.

Govern establishes leadership, accountability, and policies that enable responsible AI. Map characterizes the AI system and context of use, including stakeholders, intended use/misuse, data, and potential impacts.

Measure develops and executes test, evaluation, verification, and validation (TEVV) to quantify risks (e.g., safety, bias, robustness, privacy). Manage prioritizes risks, implements controls, monitors post-deployment, and conducts incident response and continuous improvement.

The framework emphasizes documentation (risk register, impact assessments, data statements, model/system cards), clear roles, and iterative monitoring to maintain trustworthiness over time.

• Govern (crosscutting): Define roles and accountability, risk appetite, policies, training, documentation standards, and a culture that incentivizes responsible behavior.
• Map + Measure: Map the system’s purpose, context, stakeholders, data lineage, and potential harms; then Measure with TEVV—metrics for efficacy, bias/fairness, robustness, privacy, explainability, and security (including red teaming and uncertainty analysis).
• Manage (treatment + monitoring): Prioritize risks, select and implement controls, plan change management and incident response, monitor in production, and retire/decommission safely.

• Govern sets organization-wide accountability, policies, and culture for AI risk.
• Map, Measure, and Manage work iteratively to identify context, generate evidence, and treat/monitor risks.
• Documentation, clear roles, and continuous monitoring are essential to sustaining trustworthy AI.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the NIST AI RMF functions and how to apply them across the AI lifecycle.

title.en: Controls and Evidence (NIST AI RMF & GenAI Profile)

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to design preventive, detective, and corrective controls mapped to NIST AI RMF outcomes and the GenAI Profile
- 2) What credible evidence demonstrates those controls are implemented and effective
- 3) How to tailor controls and evidence for generative AI risks such as hallucinations, jailbreaks, data leakage, and misuse

The NIST AI RMF organizes trustworthy AI practices across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. While the RMF is outcome-based (not a prescriptive control catalog), organizations implement controls to achieve those outcomes and produce evidence to demonstrate they work. The GenAI Profile specializes those outcomes for generative AI, highlighting risks like harmful content, prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucinations, intellectual property and privacy leakage, provenance of synthetic media, and misuse at scale.

Control design begins by mapping risks and desired outcomes to specific control objectives. Examples by function:
- Govern: policies, roles/RACI, model inventory, procurement/supplier clauses, documentation standards (model/data cards), accountability and training.
- Map: intended use and misuse scenarios, stakeholder impact analysis, risk appetite/tolerance, context and data lineage, legal/ethical constraints.
- Measure: evaluation suites and test plans (safety, robustness, privacy, bias), red teaming, coverage criteria, reproducibility, and acceptance thresholds.
- Manage: risk treatment plans, guardrails (content filters, tool permissioning), human-in-the-loop review, incident response, rollback/kill switches, change management, and monitoring.

GenAI control patterns:
- Preventive: access control and rate limiting; safety policies embedded in prompts; system prompt hardening; retrieval filtering; PII and IP blocklists; constrained decoding; watermarking/provenance labeling for media; content policy enforcement.
- Detective: comprehensive logging of prompts/outputs/tool calls; abuse/anomaly detection; jailbreak/prompt-injection monitors; drift and regression dashboards; shadow/canary deployments; user reporting channels.
- Corrective: automatic output blocking/quarantining; takedown workflows; rapid model/config rollback; patching/fine-tuning; incident postmortems and control updates.

Evidence must be sufficient, appropriate, current, and linked to control objectives and RMF outcomes. Strong evidence is objective, reproducible, and versioned. Typical artifacts include: policies/SOPs and training records; RACI and governance minutes; model and data cards; data lineage and license attestations; evaluation plans, test datasets, and results with pass/fail thresholds; red-team reports with methodology and remediation tracking; guardrail and filter configurations; versioned system prompts and templates; monitoring dashboards and KRIs; incident tickets and postmortems; change logs and deployment approvals; third-party assessments and supplier attestations. For GenAI, add hallucination and harmful-content benchmarks, jailbreak and prompt-injection test results, privacy leakage canaries, and provenance/watermark implementation proofs (e.g., C2PA signing and verification logs).

• Control mapping: Tie each control to a specific AI RMF outcome and GenAI risk.
• Control types: Preventive, detective, and corrective layers reduce residual risk.
• Evidence quality: Versioned, reproducible, linked to acceptance criteria and retained per policy.

• Map layered controls to AI RMF outcomes and GenAI-specific risks.
• Produce versioned, reproducible evidence tied to acceptance criteria and remediation.
• Prioritize preventive, then detective and corrective controls, validated by rigorous evaluation and red teaming.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design RMF-aligned controls for GenAI systems and assemble credible evidence to demonstrate effectiveness.

title.en: Continuous Risk Management (NIST AI RMF & GenAI Profile)

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to operationalize continuous risk management across Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage 2) How to monitor GenAI-specific risks with metrics, thresholds, and triggers 3) How to run change, incident, and improvement cycles with evidence updates

Risk in AI systems changes with data, models, users, and adversaries. The AI RMF emphasizes iteration: continually reassess context (Map), update measurements (Measure), and implement responses (Manage) under clear governance (Govern). For GenAI, continuous management must track misuse patterns (jailbreaks, prompt injection), model regressions (toxicity, hallucinations), privacy leakage, distributional shifts, and supply chain updates (new model releases, API behavior changes).

Key practices:
- Define KRIs and acceptance thresholds tied to RMF outcomes (e.g., harmful-content rate, hallucination rate on canonical tasks, refusal precision/recall, jailbreak success rate, PII leakage indicators, provenance adoption rate). Instrument telemetry and dashboards.
- Establish triggers and gates: pre-release evaluation gates; canary/shadowing; automatic rollback/kill switch when thresholds breach; incident severities and on-call runbooks.
- Run a risk register with owners, mitigations, and residual risk rationales; review regularly with cross-functional governance (legal, security, privacy, product, and domain experts).
- Maintain evaluation pipelines and data: update red-team corpora, injection/jailbreak test sets, and safety metrics as attackers evolve; validate reproducibility and coverage.
- Manage changes: version models/prompts/tools; document diffs and expected risk deltas; require approvals; update user docs and model/data cards.
- Learn from operations: analyze incidents and near-misses; implement corrective/preventive actions; recalibrate thresholds and controls; refresh training.
- External watch: track standards, regulations, supplier/model updates, and threat intelligence; adjust controls and evidence accordingly.

• KRIs and thresholds: Quantify risk and define objective triggers.
• Monitoring and telemetry: Capture prompts, outputs, tool calls, and guardrail outcomes with privacy-aware logging.
• Change and incident management: Gates, runbooks, rollback, postmortems, and continuous improvement.

• Continuous risk management requires defined KRIs, thresholds, and automated triggers tied to RMF outcomes.
• Maintain evaluation pipelines, red teaming, and change/incident management to adapt to evolving GenAI risks.
• Update governance artifacts and evidence with every significant change, incident, or shift in context.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now implement continuous, RMF-aligned risk management for generative AI systems.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How the EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk tiers (prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, minimal-risk) and what each tier requires
- 2) How to determine whether your system falls under Annex II or Annex III high-risk categories, or is subject only to transparency duties
- 3) Practical steps to document classification, select the correct conformity assessment route, and prepare evidence for audit and market surveillance.

blocks.title: Deep Dive into the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic AI Applications
blocks.label: Course Video

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
The EU AI Act applies a risk-based approach. Prohibited practices (e.g., social scoring by public authorities; untargeted scraping of facial images to build or expand facial recognition databases; manipulative systems that materially distort a person’s behavior and cause harm) are banned.

High-risk systems include (a) AI safety components covered by sectoral product safety law in Annex II (e.g., medical devices, machinery, automotive) and (b) use-cases in Annex III (e.g., biometric identification; critical infrastructure; education and exams; employment and worker management; access to essential services like credit; law enforcement; migration/asylum; administration of justice). Limited-risk systems trigger transparency duties (e.g., informing users they are interacting with AI; disclosure for emotion recognition/biometric categorization; clear labeling of AI-generated or synthetic content).

Minimal-risk systems (e.g., spam filters, AI in games) are largely unaffected but encouraged to follow voluntary codes. Classification hinges on the intended purpose defined by the provider.

To classify: 1) define intended purpose and users, 2) check Annex II/III listings, 3) if not high-risk, check if transparency obligations apply, 4) otherwise treat as minimal-risk. High-risk providers must implement a quality and risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity controls, pass conformity assessment, affix CE marking, register in the EU database, and run post-market monitoring and incident reporting.

Deployers of high-risk systems must use the system per instructions, perform data input checks, monitor performance, ensure human oversight, and keep logs.

• Intended purpose drives risk tier: map your AI to Annex II/III before assuming "limited" or "minimal".
• High-risk = life-cycle controls: QMS, risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight, logging, conformity assessment, CE marking, and post-market monitoring.
• Transparency for limited-risk: inform users of AI interaction, disclose emotion/biometric categorization, and label deepfakes/synthetic media.

• Classification starts with intended purpose, then Annex II/III mapping.
• High-risk status triggers life-cycle requirements, conformity assessment, CE marking, and registration.
• Limited-risk systems require clear user disclosure and synthetic content labeling; minimal-risk are largely unaffected.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how the EU AI Act’s risk-based model works and can classify AI systems and plan the appropriate compliance pathway.

title.en: AI literacy, transparency and GPAI obligations

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) What the EU AI Act expects on AI literacy for providers, deployers, and affected personnel
- 2) When and how to meet transparency duties (AI interaction notices, emotion/biometric categorization notices, deepfake/synthetic content labeling)
- 3) Core obligations for general-purpose AI (GPAI) model providers, including documentation, copyright compliance, training data summaries, content provenance, and systemic risk controls.

AI literacy: The Act requires providers and deployers to ensure appropriate AI literacy of staff involved in the design, development, deployment, use, and oversight of AI systems. Organizations should provide role-based training, clear instructions for use, escalation paths, and records of competence; Member States and the Commission promote broader public AI literacy.

Transparency: Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system (e.g., chatbots); natural persons must be notified when emotion recognition or biometric categorization is used; AI-generated or synthetically altered content (“deepfakes”) must be clearly labeled unless a lawful exception applies (e.g., for law enforcement or legitimate expression, provided safeguards are in place). GPAI obligations: Providers of GPAI models must prepare technical documentation for downstream providers; publish a sufficiently detailed summary of training data used (respecting trade secrets and confidentiality); put in place policies and technical measures to respect EU copyright (e.g., honoring text and data mining opt-outs and maintaining a data-use policy); implement reasonable cybersecurity and content provenance measures enabling detection of AI-generated content.

GPAI models with systemic risk (very capable models meeting objective criteria) must additionally conduct and document model evaluations and adversarial testing/red-teaming, assess and mitigate systemic risks, monitor and report serious incidents, and cooperate with the EU AI Office.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How the EU AI Act defines high-risk AI and the obligations that apply
- 2) The mandatory controls: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity
- 3) Practical steps to implement and evidence compliance, including quality management, conformity assessment, and post-market monitoring

Under the EU AI Act, high-risk AI systems (e.g., in creditworthiness, employment, essential services, education, migration, law enforcement, medical devices) must meet a comprehensive set of requirements before being placed on the market or put into service. Core obligations include: (1) Risk management system (Article 9): a documented, iterative process that identifies reasonably foreseeable risks across the lifecycle, defines risk acceptance criteria, tests mitigation measures, and feeds findings into post-market monitoring. (2) Data governance and data quality (Article 10): training, validation, and testing data must be relevant, representative, free of errors as far as possible, and complete for the intended purpose; with documented provenance, bias management, and gap analysis. (3) Technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV): a dossier describing the system, intended purpose, design and development process, data and model characteristics, performance metrics and limitations, risk controls, human oversight design, cybersecurity measures, and conformity assessment evidence. (4) Record keeping (Article 12): automatic logging to enable traceability, incident investigation, and monitoring proportional to risks and state of the art. (5) Transparency and provision of information to users (Article 13): clear instructions for use, system capabilities and limitations, expected accuracy, input data requirements, and human oversight instructions. (6) Human oversight (Article 14): design and procedures that enable trained persons to understand, appropriately monitor, override, or stop the system to prevent or minimize risks. (7) Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Article 15): defined performance targets, resilience to errors and attempts to manipulate the system, fallback plans, and secure development practices.

Providers must implement a quality management system, undergo the applicable conformity assessment (often internal control or third-party assessment depending on the module and sectoral rules), affix CE marking, register high-risk systems in the EU database, and operate a post-market monitoring and serious incident reporting process.

• Risk management system: Continuous identification, analysis, testing, and mitigation of risks across the AI lifecycle, feeding into post-market monitoring.
• Data governance and quality: Controls to ensure relevant, representative, and sufficiently complete data; documented provenance, bias testing, and data handling.
• Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity: Defined performance thresholds, stress/adversarial testing, fallback/rollback plans, and secure-by-design controls.

• High-risk AI must comply with risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity requirements.
• Providers need a quality management system, conformity assessment, CE marking, and post-market monitoring with incident reporting.
• Evidence of compliance should be built into development and operations, producing auditable artifacts aligned to Annex IV and Articles 9–15.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core high-risk requirements and how to apply them in practice.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) What technical documentation is required for high-risk AI under Annex IV 2) How logging and record-keeping enable traceability, investigation, and monitoring 3) How to design effective human oversight to prevent or minimize risks

Technical documentation (Article 11 and Annex IV) must provide a comprehensive, auditable description of the AI system and its lifecycle: intended purpose and system description; design specifications and development process; training/validation/testing data characteristics and governance measures; model architecture and configurations; performance metrics, evaluation procedures, and known limitations; risk management outcomes and mitigations; human oversight design and instructions; cybersecurity and robustness controls; post-market monitoring plan; versioning and change history; and conformity assessment evidence (including applicable harmonized standards). Documentation should be kept up to date and made available to competent authorities upon request.

Record-keeping and logging (Article 12) require high-risk systems to automatically log events relevant to their operation, proportionate to the system’s context and risks. Typical logs include input and output records, model/version identifiers, timestamps, triggered thresholds, overrides, user actions, and error states.

Logs must support traceability, incident analysis, and monitoring, and be stored securely with integrity protections and appropriate retention consistent with sectoral laws (e.g., data protection). Human oversight (Article 14) requires system design and procedures that enable natural persons to understand capabilities/limitations, detect anomalies, and effectively intervene—by disregarding, correcting, overriding, or stopping operation when needed.

Oversight includes clear user interfaces, alerts/thresholds, interpretability aids proportional to risks, training for overseers, and organizational protocols that minimize automation bias and escalation delay.

• Technical documentation (Annex IV): A complete, current dossier covering purpose, data, model, performance, risks, oversight, cybersecurity, and conformity evidence.
• Logging and traceability (Article 12): Automated, tamper-resistant event logs capturing inputs/outputs, versions, timestamps, and interventions to enable audits and incident investigation.
• Human oversight (Article 14): Design and procedures that equip trained people to understand outputs, detect issues, and override or stop the system safely.

• Annex IV technical documentation must be complete, current, and auditable across purpose, data, model, performance, risks, and oversight.
• Logging must enable traceability and incident investigation with secure, proportionate, integrity-protected records and governed retention.
• Human oversight requires design and training that empower people to understand, monitor, and safely intervene in system operation.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand documentation, logging, and human oversight requirements and how to implement them.

body.en:
An AI system registry is a centralized inventory of all AI/ML systems, models, datasets, and related services across the organization. It provides traceability from business purpose to technical artifacts and operational controls, enabling compliance, risk assessment, and rapid incident handling.

Scope and purpose: The registry covers models (including LLMs and fine-tunes), datasets, pipelines, prompts/agents, evaluation suites, deployments, and downstream integrations that act on AI outputs. It links to owners, approvers, and on-call contacts to support accountability.

Regulatory alignment: A registry supports obligations in GDPR (Records of Processing Activities when personal data is processed), the EU AI Act (risk classification, technical documentation, post-market monitoring), sector rules (e.g., model governance in finance/health), and frameworks like NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 AI management systems.

Minimum critical fields: Business purpose and allowed use; system owner and accountable executive; risk classification and justification; data categories (PII, sensitive attributes, special categories); training and evaluation datasets with lineage; model provenance and version/commit hash; deployment environments and endpoints; access controls and consumer apps; human-in-the-loop/override; pre-deployment reviews (privacy impact/DPIA, algorithmic impact assessments); evaluation results (performance, robustness, bias/fairness); red-teaming outcomes; monitoring metrics and alert thresholds; incident runbook, rollback/kill-switch location; vendor dependencies and licenses; change history and approvals.

Lifecycle and automation: Create entries at proposal stage, update at each material change, and retire with archival of artifacts and logs. Enforce completeness via CI/CD gates (e.g., block deployment if mandatory fields or risk reviews are missing). Auto-populate fields from MLOps (model registries, feature stores), IaC (environments, endpoints), and security tooling (SBOM/MBOM, vulnerability scans). Tag releases and pin versions for reproducibility.

Incident response linkage: The registry must make it easy to find on-call contacts, affected services, last safe version, and rollback steps. It should store monitoring metrics, evaluation baselines, and known failure modes to accelerate triage. Access should be searchable and permissioned, with audit logs of who changed what and when.

• Single source of truth: A centralized, authoritative inventory that links business purpose to technical and risk artifacts
• Risk-critical metadata: Owner/on-call, data categories, evaluations, red-team results, versioning, and kill-switch details enable fast audits and incident response
• Lifecycle integration: CI/CD and MLOps automation keep entries current and enforce governance before deployment

• Maintain a centralized registry linking business purpose, risk, and technical artifacts
• Capture risk-critical metadata (owners, data categories, evaluations, red-team results, versions, kill switch)
• Automate updates via CI/CD/MLOps and use deploy gates to enforce completeness and approvals
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to build and operate an AI system registry that enables compliance, auditability, and fast incident response.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to assess and onboard external AI vendors and models 2) Which contractual, security, and compliance controls reduce third-party and model risk 3) How to monitor vendors/models and coordinate incident response and continuity

Vendor and model risk management ensures third-party AI services and external models meet organizational, security, and regulatory requirements.

Due diligence: Evaluate use case risk, data sensitivity, and impact. Review vendor security posture (SOC 2 Type II, ISO/IEC 27001), AI governance maturity (alignment to NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001), privacy practices (DPA, data residency, cross-border transfers), and incident response processes (RACI, notification SLAs). Verify safe-by-design practices: red-teaming, safety filters, content moderation, prompt injection defenses, and abuse monitoring.

Data handling and IP: Confirm how prompts/outputs are stored, encrypted, and retained; whether data is used to train or fine-tune provider models; availability of zero-retention or customer-controlled encryption; and terms around model/IP licensing and attribution. Require restrictions on training with customer data unless explicitly allowed.

Model-specific controls: Demand model cards or equivalent documentation (intended use, limitations, evaluation metrics, bias/fairness evidence), version pinning, and change notifications. Validate robustness to known threats (prompt injection, data exfiltration, jailbreaks), and require red-team reports or your own validation before production. Track dependencies (datasets, open-source components) and provenance/attestations (signed artifacts, Model/AI BOM where available).

Contracts and SLAs: Include uptime/performance SLAs, rate limits, data protection terms, security requirements, audit/assessment rights, breach notification timelines, and required support for incident investigations. Define kill-switch/rollback options, termination assistance, and data deletion/return.

Ongoing monitoring: Continuously evaluate model quality, safety, latency, and cost. Watch for silent model updates; enforce canary testing and phased rollouts. Manage concentration risk with fallback providers and routing controls. Log vendor issues in your registry and tie to playbooks for coordinated incident response.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) Identify, triage, and classify AI incidents and near-misses 2) Execute compliant reporting to regulators, customers, and internal stakeholders 3) Design an effective post-market monitoring program with metrics, tooling, and CAPA to prevent recurrence

An AI incident is an event where an AI system causes or could reasonably cause harm (e.g., safety, financial, privacy, security, fairness, rights). Near-misses warrant learning as much as realized harms.

Establish an incident taxonomy and severity levels (e.g., SEV-1 to SEV-3) with SLAs, an incident commander, and a cross‑functional team (AI/ML, product, legal, privacy, security, compliance, comms). Preserve evidence with immutable logs, versioned models/data, and chain of custody; consider legal privilege for investigations.

Reporting obligations span internal alerts, customer notifications per contract, and regulatory rules (e.g., personal data breaches under GDPR may require notifying authorities within 72 hours; sectoral/product rules can impose additional timelines). High‑risk AI use cases should have post‑market monitoring (PMM): continuous tracking of performance, robustness, safety, and fairness using metrics such as drift, false positives/negatives, hallucination/toxicity/refusal rates, disparity ratios, and human override rates; include red teaming, canary releases, and complaint/feedback channels.

Perform root‑cause analysis (5 Whys, Fishbone) and implement CAPA—corrective fixes (rollbacks, rule/guardrail updates, access controls) and preventive measures (data curation, re‑training, process/policy updates, additional tests). Integrate with existing security incident response and SOC processes, run tabletop exercises, and document lessons learned.

Align with frameworks like NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) and ISO/IEC 23894 (risk management) and operationalize within an AI management system (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001).

• Incident taxonomy and severity: Define what counts as an AI incident/near-miss and how to classify impact and urgency.
• Reporting workflows and timelines: Clear triggers, owners, approvals, and channels for internal, customer, and regulatory notifications.
• Post-market monitoring and CAPA: Continuous metrics, feedback loops, root-cause analysis, and corrective/preventive actions to reduce recurrence.

• Define incidents, severities, roles, and SLAs; run playbooks and preserve evidence.
• Meet internal, customer, and regulatory reporting duties; align with privacy and sector rules.
• Implement PMM with metrics, feedback loops, RCA, and CAPA to continuously reduce risk.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to report AI incidents and operate a post-market monitoring program that detects, contains, and prevents harms.

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) Build concise, decision-ready executive dashboards and board packs 2) Select KPIs/KRIs and thresholds aligned to risk appetite and regulation 3) Communicate incidents, assurance results, and remediation status with clear ownership and timelines

Executive reporting translates complex AI risk and performance into decisions. A board pack should include: an AI system inventory and risk classification; a risk heat map and top risks; incident summaries and trends (e.g., SEV-1 rate, MTTD/MTTR, root causes); compliance status against applicable laws (e.g., AI use classification, privacy, sector regulations); assurance results (internal audit, external attestations, red-teaming) and control effectiveness; key KPIs/KRIs (performance vs targets, fairness disparity ratios, toxicity/hallucination rates, robustness/adversarial test coverage, monitoring coverage, model change frequency, human oversight efficacy); third‑party/foundation model risk; exceptions and waivers; resourcing, training, and budget; and forward‑looking approvals/decisions needed.

Use clear thresholds, trendlines, and traffic‑light status. Define decision rights and escalation criteria (what triggers ad‑hoc board notification vs quarterly cadence) and map RACI across management, risk, and audit committees.

Align with NIST AI RMF governance and AI management systems (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001) so board oversight matches stated risk appetite and strategy. Keep narrative plain‑language, blameless but accountable, and include a one‑page executive summary with appendices for detail.

• Board pack structure: Inventory, risk heat map, incidents/trends, compliance and assurance, decisions required, and appendices.
• KPIs/KRIs and thresholds: Metrics that reflect harm, fairness, robustness, performance, and control effectiveness with clear targets.
• Escalation and decision rights: Materiality criteria, RACI, and committee roles to act on incidents and approvals.

• Board packs should be decision-oriented: concise summaries, clear KRIs/KPIs, and explicit asks.
• Use thresholds, trends, and RACI to drive timely escalation and accountability.
• Link oversight to recognized frameworks and your AI management system to evidence control effectiveness.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now craft executive and board-ready AI risk reports that enable effective oversight and timely decisions.
